journal.hardwrought.lore.bare_hands_what: What gives way to a hand

The world does not yield to every grip. What is held decides three things: whether a block breaks at all, what it costs in stamina, and what comes out of it.

• Loose things such as leaves, plants, sand and snow are taken by a bare hand without trouble.
• Dirt, gravel and clay can be dug by hand, but at barely a third of the speed and for four times the stamina. Only a handful comes up, and only three times in four: two Dirt Clods from dirt, a Flint Shard from gravel. Clay gives a bare hand nothing at all; clay balls need a shovel.
• Glass shatters under a fist and leaves nothing.
• Rock, ore and wood do not move for a bare hand at all, however long it strikes.

The wrong tool, such as a hatchet against stone or a pickaxe against a log, works at a quarter of the speed, costs three times the stamina, takes two extra points of wear, and every second block is lost in the process. A pickaxe too soft for an ore does break it, slowly, but yields nothing.

Even with the right tool, hard material is work: stone and logs break at about 40 % of the usual speed, ore at barely a third. Every block costs stamina according to its hardness.

Flint tools last only 32 uses and stand at the rank of wood: the Flint Pickaxe breaks stone and coal, but not iron ore. The Stone Pickaxe lasts about four times as long and breaks iron, copper and tin ore.

Leaves broken with an empty hand give a Green Leaf Fibre about one time in eight; with a tool, never. And leaves carry no person: you sink slowly through them, and a fall through a tree crown is still a fall.
journal.hardwrought.lore.bare_hands_thir:
The body holds a water reserve of 100 points. Even at complete rest it falls by 0.035 a second, so a full reserve lasts less than 50 minutes; walking, work, heat and heavy armor drain it further. The emptier the reserve, the more slowly stamina comes back, in the end at only a quarter of the speed. Once it is empty, thirst costs half a heart every four seconds, and no armor helps against it.

Drinking from the hand: crouch, keep the main hand empty, and use it on water you are looking at or standing in. Each mouthful gives 10 points, at most one a second, and takes 100 mB of water out of the world; a shallow puddle runs dry eventually.

What a mouthful is worth, and how often it makes you ill, depends on the kind:
• Purified: 110 %, never ill
• Fresh (spring, rain): 100 %, 4 % a mouthful
• River: 90 %, 12 %
• Swamp: 65 %, 45 %
• Sea: minus 60 %, 5 %. Salt water takes more from the body than it gives.

The colour tells the kind: river water is a stronger blue, swamp water a murky olive, seawater grey-green, purified water light blue. The water of high meadows and cherry groves is purified by nature; such a spring is a treasure.

When waters run together, the worse kind wins as soon as it makes up a quarter of the amount. A supply is spoiled quickly and cleaned only with effort.

An unlucky mouthful does no harm at once. It gives a stomach bug: for a minute nothing is felt, then it noticeably drains your water. Drinking from the hand is therefore always a gamble, and in a swamp one lost almost every second time. Boiled water is the way out, as soon as there is a vessel for it.
journal.hardwrought.lore.bare_hands_fire:
A Campfire is always set down cold. It is lit with the Fire-lighting Sticks (they last 16 times), with Flint and Steel, or with a burning torch; one standing in water will not catch. Once lit it burns for about two days and nights and then goes out, and has to be lit again.

What a burning Campfire does:
• Warmth up to five blocks away, falling off steeply: right beside it about 13 °C more, two blocks away still about 7 °C. There is a right distance to sit at.
• Cooking as usual. A clay ball becomes a brick on it in 45 seconds.

Torches are made unlit. They are lit at anything that burns: a Campfire, fire, lava, a burning furnace, a burning torch. Or in the hand, when the other hand holds the Fire-lighting Sticks, Flint and Steel or a burning torch. An Unlit Torch can also be set down and lit only once it is on the wall.

A burning torch burns for 20 minutes, one whole day, and it burns everywhere: in the hand, in the pack, on the wall. Afterwards a stick is left. Set down, it burns only for what it had left; taken down, it carries the rest with it. Burning torches do not stack. A burnt-out torch on the wall can be lit again by the same means.

The Drying Rack holds four pieces. It dries only in daylight, under open sky and without rain; a tree crown above it counts as a roof too. Half a day of such weather turns Green Leaf Fibre into Leaf Cord. At night and in rain the work rests, but nothing is lost. Hang things up in the morning.

The Brick Furnace works at only half the speed of an ordinary furnace and gets only two thirds out of every fuel. It is a makeshift, but the only one that makes metal hot.
journal.hardwrought.lore.bare_hands_woun:
A hurt body does less. Below 60 % of its health it slows down, and the lower, the more:
• at 45 %: walking minus 6 %, digging minus 10 %, jumping minus 5 %
• at 30 %: walking minus 12 %, digging minus 20 %, jumping minus 10 %
• below that up to minus 25 %, 40 % and 20 %, and running is no longer possible at all.
Every fight makes the next one harder until the wounds have healed.

Open wounds are torn by a bite (zombies and their kin, wolves, spiders, silverfish, endermites, polar bears) or by a monster's blow of 4 damage or more. Fire, frost, drowning and magic do not open them. A light hit (4 to 6) stays open for one minute, a deep one (7 to 11) for two, a severe one (12 and more) for three; a bite counts one level worse. While it is open, dirt can get in, over the whole time about 1 in 20, 1 in 4 or 2 in 3. That becomes an inflamed wound with fever and weakness. A bandage closes a wound for five minutes; a new bite tears it off again.

Diseases run a course. At first nothing is felt (a minute for the stomach, a minute and a half for a wound, two for a cold), then the illness grows and fades by itself if the body is looked after. Sleep helps three times as well, standing still a little; thirst, hunger and a body too cold or too hot slow the healing. Whoever neglects it sees it turn severe and take its worse name; once critical, any disease costs health every 20 seconds. Once it is over, you are proof against it for ten minutes.

Two minutes chilled, or wet and cool, and you have a cold. Raw meat can upset the stomach: raw chicken three times in ten, rotten flesh every second time.

There is a grace period: outside Ultra mode you are proof against everything for 40 minutes on first entering a world and after every death. That is the time to find good water.
journal.hardwrought.lore.first_iron_heat:
Raw iron does not melt into a bar in a furnace: every furnace only heats forge metal. The whole stack in the input comes out at once, as hot as furnaces get: 1550 °C, just past the melting point of iron. In the Brick Furnace this takes ten seconds, and one piece of coal lasts about five loads there. Nothing that melts hotter than iron is taken by any furnace.

Forging heat is a share of the melting point, 55 to 85 %. For iron (1538 °C) that means:
• above 1307 °C: too hot. A head or a blade struck like that loses quality.
• 846 to 1307 °C: the right heat.
• below 846 °C: cold. The hammer moves nothing, and the blow does not count.

In the air metal cools steadily, fast at first and then more slowly. Fresh from the furnace, iron is too hot for a good ten seconds and then workable for a little under half a minute. Every blow of the hammer takes another 6 °C. When the piece is too cold, it goes back into the furnace: the work stays in the piece, even for hours.

Above 60 °C metal burns a bare hand, 2 damage every second for as long as it lies in either hand. In the pack it does no harm. The Smithing Gloves go into the glove slot of your equipment, not into the hand; wearing them, glowing metal may be held. Iron takes almost four minutes to go cold from furnace heat.

Hot pieces stack with equally hot pieces of the same kind, but not with cold ones. Only below 50 °C do they lose their heat and join the rest.

A tip: set out the anvil first, then heat. Whoever still has to look for the hammer after the furnace is left holding cold iron.
journal.hardwrought.lore.first_iron_anvi:
Hammer in the main hand, the glowing piece in the off hand, then use the anvil. If the piece can become several things, a bar can become any head, the anvil asks first and shows what each costs:
• axe head and pickaxe head: three bars each
• hoe head and sword blade: two
• shovel head and dagger blade: one
One lump of raw iron gives exactly one bar. All the bars of a head are taken at the start and worked as one piece in the off hand.

The piece appears eight times enlarged, one square per pixel, with the target shape faintly behind it. Every click is a blow: what stands proud is driven in, gaps are filled. The Wooden Hammer covers exactly one square. A blow where everything is already right is wasted.

Heads and blades carry a quality that comes from the blows: a base of 20 %, plus up to 55 % for accuracy (useful blows over all blows) and up to 25 % for economy (how close the number of blows came to a third of the wrong squares). Blows on metal that is too hot pull the result down, by up to half if every blow was too hot. With the Wooden Hammer, which covers a single square, full economy is impossible; no more than about 83 % can be had that way. A bar carries no quality; how well it was struck does not matter.

The Wooden Anvil allows at most 85 % quality. It wears: every finished piece costs it two points, and on average every twelfth blow one more; at 24 points it splits, so after twelve pieces at most. Cracks show how far it has gone. The hammer suffers too: about every fourth blow costs it a point, and every blow a little stamina.

Giving up returns everything that went in, as hot as it is now. A half-finished piece shows its shape so far in the pack, with a bar for its progress.
journal.hardwrought.lore.first_iron_qual:
A head or a blade carries its quality from the anvil and hands it on to the finished tool when it is put together with sticks. What the tool is worth follows from it:
• mining speed: 80 % plus 30 % times quality
• durability: 65 % plus 60 % times quality
• damage: 85 % plus 25 % times quality
At 50 % quality a tool falls just short of an ordinary one; at the 85 % a Wooden Anvil allows it digs a good 5 % faster and lasts 16 % longer. A tool nobody forged, from a chest for instance, is exactly ordinary.

Quenching: an iron part still hotter than 692 °C (45 % of the melting point) is hardened when it falls into water. Simply throw it into a river, a lake or a cauldron of water; it is cold at once. The steam costs water: one layer (125 mB) of open water, or one level of the cauldron. From furnace heat there is a little under a minute before the iron drops below that line. A head that has grown too cool after long work can go back into the furnace once more and then into the water.

Hardened means: mining times 1.10, damage times 1.08, but durability times 0.75. Hard and sharp, but brittle. If a hardened part is heated above 692 °C again, the hardening is gone.

Only iron takes a hardening. Copper, gold and bronze come out of the water as soft as they went in.

Whether to harden is a choice. For a pickaxe that should dig fast it is worth it; whoever would rather forge anew less often lets the part cool in the air. There is also a way to take the brittleness out again and keep most of the hardness, but it needs a gentler, controllable glow than a Brick Furnace has.
journal.hardwrought.lore.first_iron_soun:
Crouch and use a pickaxe on natural ground: stone, dirt, sand, gravel or terracotta. Built walls tell nothing. Every sounding first names the kind of rock, because that decides what lies in it:
• Granite: iron (between Y minus 50 and 70), gold further down
• Volcanic rock: copper above all (Y minus 40 to 80), redstone in the depths
• Sedimentary rock: coal, copper, lapis lazuli, tin (Y minus 40 to 90), lead and zinc

Ore lies in large bodies, not in scattered lumps. Standing inside such a body, the sounding tells how rich the rock is at that spot, as a grade in percent. Otherwise a flint or stone pickaxe names the nearest ore within 48 blocks, but not where it lies. An iron pickaxe reads far more: the nearest body up to 160 blocks away, with its rough distance, the direction and the height of its middle. That alone makes the first iron pickaxe worth having.

The grade pays. For every full twelfth, about 8.3 % each, every ore block gives its yield once more, at most four times extra. At a 25 % grade a block of iron ore therefore yields four times as much raw iron as one at the rim. The middle of a body is richer than its edge; it pays to follow the grade rather than take the first lump and move on.

For iron ore the Stone Pickaxe is enough; the flint one only scratches at it and brings nothing out. A long tunnel at the right height, driven straight through a body, opens up more ore than many small holes.
journal.hardwrought.lore.bench_and_bronz:
Every recipe needs a minimum rung, and there are three:
• The grid in your own hands, two by two: only the first things, such as flint tools, sticks, planks, torches, the Campfire, the Brick Furnace, the Wooden Anvil and tools put together from head and handle.
• The Hewn Workbench, three by three: wood, stone, flint and fibre, but no metal. Shaft, Hand Crank, crusher, bowl, Stone Hammer, Bronze Mixture, chests, ladders and the like.
• The Nailed Workbench: everything a workbench can make at all. Whatever no rung names explicitly needs this one.
An old crafting table found in the world falls apart when used.

Hewing: crouch against a standing log with an axe of at least iron rank and hold the use button; every repetition is a stroke. Flint, stone and gold will not do. An iron axe needs about eight to ten strokes, fewer the faster the axe, but never fewer than eight. Pause for five seconds and the strokes counted so far are forgotten. Every stroke costs stamina, and the finished bench costs the axe four points. Crouching never strips the bark off a log.

Nailing: Bronze Nails in the pack or the off hand, any hammer in the main hand, and hold the use button on the Hewn Workbench. It takes 16 blows, about three seconds. Pause for three seconds and it starts over. Only the last blow uses up one bundle of nails and costs the hammer four points. The kind of wood is kept.

The Nailed Workbench keeps what lies in its grid when it is closed; a half-laid recipe waits for the next visit.

A tip for the anvil: the Stone Hammer (two Cobblestone Pieces, cord and two sticks) covers two by two squares. Only with it can you forge economically enough to reach the full 85 % of the Wooden Anvil.

An empty bowl dipped into water holds 250 mB, and takes the water as it is: swamp stays swamp.

Boiling: lay the Bowl of Water on a burning Campfire like food. After 20 seconds the water is purified, whether it came from a river, a swamp or a spring. The Campfire refuses seawater, because boiling only makes it saltier. Water already purified, or still hot, is not set on again either.

Cooling: the bowl comes off the fire boiling hot. In the pack or in the hand it cools over 30 seconds; the orange bar under it is the heat going out of it, and it steams until then. It can be drunk at any time, but:
• If it is still hotter than a third, that is within the first 20 seconds, it scalds: 2 to 4 damage at once and a minute of Scalded, in the first few seconds even a severe one.
• A scald can become inflamed; over its minute this happens more than every second time, except during the grace period. It turns into an inflamed wound with fever and weakness.
Waiting ten seconds longer is the cheaper way.

What it is worth: a bowl gives 22 points of water times the worth of the kind, so a good 24 when purified. A mouthful from the hand gives only 10, and purified water never makes you ill. Drinking takes as long as a potion; the empty bowl is left and can be filled again at once.

With two or three bowls at the fire you can boil a small supply while doing other things. Purified water that has gone cold stays purified for as long as it stays in the bowl.

The Starter Crusher grinds one lump into one powder. It takes raw iron, raw copper and raw gold, Raw Tin and the other raw metals, finished ingots too (back into powder), coal and charcoal (into Coal Powder) and lapis lazuli. Use the stack in your hand on the crusher to put it in; with an empty hand you take the powder out, and if there is none yet, the ore comes back. Hoppers fill it from the top and the sides and draw from the bottom.

Drive: the crusher works only while it is turned. It takes the turning from any side: from the end of a shaft pointing into it, or from a crank set directly on it. The Hand Crank drives only the one face it was mounted on. Hold the use button on the crank; every repetition is a stroke, keeps it going for a moment and costs a little stamina. Five strokes a second tire you about twice as much as sprinting. Let go and the shaft winds down.

The crank turns at 16 revolutions a minute; that is exactly what the crusher is built for, and at that speed it takes four seconds per lump. One crank carries exactly one crusher, not two. If the drive stops, the half-ground lump stays in the jaws until it goes on. When the output is full, the crusher stands still.

Why powder? Powder is cast instead of forged. In a furnace, iron or copper powder melts straight into an ingot, with no anvil and no quality to spoil. Tin Powder even melts on a Campfire, in a minute. And only ground can metals be mixed into an alloy.

Two logs stacked on top of each other make four shafts; one shaft serves the crusher, another the crank.

Bronze is three parts copper to one part tin. At the Hewn Workbench, three Copper Powder and one Tin Powder make four Bronze Mixture, one per powder.

Copper is green-veined stone, found mostly in volcanic rock but also in sedimentary rock; the Stone Pickaxe is enough.

Tin comes two ways:
• Tin Ore in sedimentary rock, between Y minus 40 and 90, also with the Stone Pickaxe. The Raw Tin goes into the crusher.
• Gravel: whoever breaks gravel with a tool, the Flint Shovel for instance, finds a Raw Tin in about every twentieth block. Dug by bare hands, gravel gives only Flint Shards.

Casting: Bronze Mixture is not forged but melted. On a Campfire one ingot takes a minute, in the Brick Furnace 20 seconds. Bronze melts at only 950 °C.

Forging: bronze can be worked from about 520 °C up to about 810 °C. It comes out of the furnace at 1550 °C, far above that. For nails this does no harm, but for heads every blow struck too hot costs quality: so wait a good 40 seconds after the furnace, and then there is a little under half a minute to strike. Bronze takes no hardening.

What bronze is good for:
• Bronze Nails: one Bronze Ingot, drawn out hot on the anvil, gives one bundle, enough for a workbench.
• Bronze Pickaxe Head and Bronze Axe Head, three ingots each, become the Bronze Pickaxe and Bronze Hatchet with a handle. They stand at the rank of iron, dig just as fast and last 375 uses, more than ordinary iron with 250.

Choosing between iron and bronze: iron is easier to find, bronze lasts longer. For the first good pickaxe either will do.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_workshop_wo:
Only what cuts or bites opens a wound: a bite (a zombie and its kin, a wolf, spider, silverfish, endermite or polar bear) of one point of damage or more, or a monster's blow of four or more. Fire, frost, drowning and magic open none. How bad it is follows the blow, and a bite counts one level worse:

• I, superficial (4 to 6): open for a minute, about 1 in 20 that dirt gets in
• II, deep (7 to 11): two minutes, about 1 in 4
• III, severe (12 and up): three minutes, about 2 in 3

A bandage closes the wound against dirt for five minutes; a new bite or blow tears it off. Three leaf string make two bandages, a block of wool four.

Every illness first takes hold unnoticed: a stomach bug for a minute, an inflamed wound for a minute and a half, a cold for two. Then its load grows. From 50 it bears its worse name (dysentery, pneumonia, blood poisoning); from 80 it is critical and costs a point of health every 20 seconds. An inflamed wound already eats a point every 30 seconds from 60, though never below three hearts. The sick grow hungry half again as fast, tire sooner and get their breath back slower. Once it is over, one is proof against that illness for ten minutes.

The body heals itself if it is helped. What speeds recovery:

• sleeping three times, standing still by a third
• chamomile tea three times, against the stomach
• willow bark tea twice, against a cold or a wound; it brings the fever down to 40 percent

Bad thirst or hunger, and a body too cold or too hot, slow it. A tea works for five minutes; the infusion boils in 20 seconds on a campfire. Every second birch log the axe strips drops willow bark.

A cold is caught by staying two minutes below 35.5 degrees of body heat, or wet and below 36.5.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_workshop_wa:
Not all water is alike. What a drink is worth, and how often it makes one ill:

• Purified: 110 percent, never
• Fresh (spring, rain): 100 percent, 4 drinks in 100
• River: 90 percent, 12 in 100
• Swamp: 65 percent, 45 in 100
• Salt: takes more than it gives (minus 60 percent)

What it gives is a stomach bug. When two waters mix, the worse one decides as soon as it makes up a quarter: one bucket of seawater spoils a tank. Boiling purifies everything but seawater, which it only makes saltier. A bowl holds 250 mB; fresh off the fire it is hot and cools in 30 seconds. Drunk too hot, it scalds.

A filter takes water poured in on top and gives it out cleaned underneath, at most 50 mB a tick each way: into a tank below, or onto the ground. Each side holds four buckets. Buckets fill and empty it, an empty bowl dips out a bowlful, and an empty hand shows what stands in it. A filter can simply stand under a spring.

• Sand filter: 50 mB a second, a bucket in 20 seconds. River and swamp water become fresh water; seawater it does not take at all. One piece of charcoal lasts four buckets, and the bed holds charcoal for 16.
• Ceramic filter: 150 mB a second. Anything but seawater comes out purified. One piece of charcoal lasts 16 buckets, and the bed holds charcoal for 64.

With no charcoal in the bed nothing runs through. Purified water stays clean only while it stays in a bucket, bowl or tank; poured onto the ground beside other water, it mixes and is spoiled again.

Now and then clean water is found by itself: in meadows, cherry groves and groves even the spring is purified.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_workshop_fo:
Coal in a forge does not catch by itself; flint and steel, a fire charge or lighting sticks light it. After that the fire takes the next coal as each burns down, and each lasts four times as long as in a furnace. The fire rises slowly and the pieces follow it slowly; while it burns they keep their heat, and one can take them out one at a time. A single forge has one place for coal and one for metal; four set as a flat square have one and four, nine as three by three have four and nine.

On its own a forge reaches about 1300 degrees, with a bellows beside it turned by a crank or a shaft 2000 degrees. Coal burnt in a closed room fills it with carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide. A forge hood one to three blocks above the bed catches the fumes over its own block and the eight around it; one is enough for three by three.

Iron melts at 1538 degrees and forges between about 850 and 1300. Below that a blow does nothing. Above it the metal still moves, but every blow on an overheated part costs quality, up to half. A forge without bellows therefore cannot overheat iron; with one, take it out in time. Every blow costs the piece 6 degrees.

Hardening: an iron part, hotter than about 690 degrees, thrown into water or a water cauldron. The steam takes a little water with it.
• quenched: digs 10 percent faster, hits 8 percent harder, but lasts only three quarters as long
• then tempered, warmed back to 185 to 460 degrees: 6 percent faster, 5 percent harder and 12 percent more durable

A hardened piece heated past 690 degrees again is as soft as before. Bronze, copper and gold do not harden. Without smithing gloves hot metal burns the hand.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_workshop_sh:
Everything joined by shafts, cogwheels and belts makes one line. Every part turns at a fixed ratio to every other; a large cogwheel on a cogwheel turns half as fast as it. So a line has one speed, in turns per minute (RPM).

Sources give speed and strength, machines take strength: their load per RPM times the speed they run at. Gearing a machine faster makes it heavier to turn as well. A line asked for more strength than its sources give is overstressed and stands still. Two sources turning against each other jam it.

• Hand crank: 16 RPM, strength 160, while it is cranked
• Starter crusher: load 8 per RPM, so 128 on a crank; one fits, two do not. At 16 RPM a chunk takes four seconds, at 32 two.
• Bellows: load 4 per RPM

A water wheel turns on a horizontal axle and is three blocks across. Each of the eight cells around the hub that holds water pushes with its current along the way the paddle there moves. Set across a river with its lower paddles in the water, it turns; set along it, not; in still water, never. Water falling past one side drives it like an overshot wheel. A solid block in any of the eight cells jams it. It gives up to 32 RPM and up to 768 strength, about 460 with three paddles in a river.

A windmill's sails sweep five by five blocks. With less than 60 percent of that open air they stand still, and every block in the way costs wind. Wind grows with height: full strength 64 blocks above the sea, three times that 192 above, down to a quarter below. Rain adds a quarter, a thunderstorm 60 percent. Over five minutes it swells and falls, in each region at its own moment. A mill gives 4 to 24 RPM and up to 1024 strength.
journal.hardwrought.lore.smeltery_and_st:
Two clay balls, sand and gravel make two fireclay; fired in a furnace, each becomes a refractory brick. From these, at the bench:

• Smeltery bricks: 4 bricks
• Smeltery glass: 4 bricks around a glass
• Smeltery controller: 8 bricks
• Smeltery drain: 6 bricks
• Casting table: 7 bricks
• Faucet: 3 bricks
• Smeltery tank: 8 bricks around a glass

The heart of a smeltery is a box of air, its tank: up to seven by seven blocks and eight high. Under every block of it there must be smeltery bricks. Round it, on every layer, runs a ring of wall: smeltery bricks, smeltery glass, drains, tanks and the controller. The corners of the ring may be left out. A layer counts only while its ring is whole from the floor up; a gap cuts off everything above it, and the controller has to sit in a layer that counts, facing out.

Every block of the tank holds eight bars, 1152 mB. A tank three by three and two high therefore holds 144 bars.

The drain sits in the wall; a faucet hangs on its outside, and the casting table stands right under the faucet. Bellows against any wall block fan the fire, but only while a hand crank or a turning shaft works them.

The smeltery checks its build every second. If a piece breaks out of the wall, it goes out until it stands again. The controller has one place for fuel and 27 for what is to melt.

Refractory brick serves the forge too: eight of them in hand, used on a forge, line it once and for good. Lined, it reaches 1600 degrees, with bellows 2800.

How hot a smeltery gets depends on its fuel, and on whether bellows blow:

• Coal or charcoal: 1250 degrees, with bellows 1650
• Coke: 2000 degrees, with bellows 4200
• Lava from a smeltery tank: 1600 degrees, with bellows 2000

Coke is coal fired in a furnace; nine make a block of coke, and it gives them back. Burn time in the smeltery: coal one minute, coke two, a block of coal nine, a block of coke eighteen minutes. A smeltery tank in the wall holds four buckets of lava; tanks side by side make one vessel. Lava burns only while the fuel place is empty: 50 mB every 15 seconds, so a bucket lasts five minutes. The heat rises and falls slowly towards the fire's.

A metal melts only once the tank stands at its full melting point:

• Tin 232 degrees
• Bronze 950 degrees
• Gold 1064 degrees
• Copper 1085 degrees
• Iron 1538 degrees

So coal alone melts copper, tin, bronze and gold, iron never. Iron wants coal with bellows, or coke.

What goes in gives:

• a bar, plate, raw ore or ore powder: 144 mB
• a nugget: 16 mB, a rod: 36 mB
• a whole ore block: 288 mB, twice the raw ore
• a block of nine bars or raw ore: 1296 mB

A bar takes five seconds once the tank is hot enough; small things go faster, a block takes half a minute. Coal powder dissolves into the bath as carbon from 1000 degrees, 72 mB a powder.

Whatever lies in the tank alloys as soon as it is hot enough, 4 mB a tick. Three parts copper and one part tin become four parts bronze at 1085 degrees.

Four fireclay at the bench make an unfired ingot cast; fired in a furnace it becomes an ingot cast. For every other part there is a cast blank of four fireclay in a square. Lay the blank on the casting table and click it with a bar or a finished part: the piece is not used up, and the blank takes its shape. Take it off and fire it in a furnace. The first part of a kind therefore has to be forged; the cast copies it, and from then on takes any metal that has such a part.

A click on the faucet opens it. It pours the lowest metal in the tank, 8 mB a tick, until the cast is full: 144 mB for a bar, and for a part as many bars as it costs at the anvil, a pickaxe head three. Which metal lies lowest is chosen in the controller's window: clicking a layer moves it to the bottom. If there is no such part of that metal, nothing runs, and the faucet says why. After two seconds the casting has set and comes out at 70 percent of its melting point, glowing: wear gloves.

A hopper under the casting table draws out what has set and leaves the cast. A redstone signal on the faucet pours again as soon as the cast is empty; the two together cast bars into a chest until the metal runs out.

A cast part is rough: 20 percent quality. A grindstone finishes it, and any forged part too. Click the grindstone with the part in the main hand, then hold the mouse button or the space bar: the marker climbs, and letting go lets it fall. A green band with a gold middle wanders; a pass lasts three seconds. How much of it the marker spent in the band (the middle in full, the rest at 72 percent):

• 85 percent and up: plus 5 points of quality
• from 62: plus 3, from 35: plus 1
• below that: a scratch, minus 2

A part takes eight passes, at most plus 40. A cast part ends at 60 percent; a perfectly forged one reaches 140.

Steel is made only in the bath. Four parts iron and one part carbon become four parts steel from 1540 degrees, 4 mB a tick. The carbon comes from coal powder, which the crusher grinds from coal or charcoal: one powder to two iron bars gives two steel bars. Whatever is left over, iron or carbon, lies in the tank as a layer of its own. The bath has to be hot enough: coal with bellows (1650 degrees), or coke.

Steel melts at 1450 degrees and forges between about 800 and 1230. A forge without bellows climbs to 1300, a little too hot: take steel out in time, or every blow costs quality. A freshly cast steel bar leaves the casting table at a little over 1000 degrees and can go straight to the anvil. Steel hardens like iron: quenched from above about 650 degrees, tempered at 175 to 435.

What steel gives over iron:

• durability 900 instead of 250
• mining speed 7.5 instead of 6
• one point more damage
• it mines what diamond mines, obsidian too

A pickaxe head cast, once pressed, takes steel too. A cast head is quickly made but rough; the grindstone brings it to 60 percent at most, and a well forged head stands above it.

Steel rusts. A steel tool, weapon or piece of armor held or worn in rain or water is fully rusted after about four minutes of being wet. At full rust a tool digs at only 60 percent and a weapon hits at 70, and every use may wear it a second time, the likelier the rustier it is. The tooltip shows the rust. Clicking a grindstone with it takes the rust off, and two percent of its durability with it.
journal.hardwrought.lore.runes_and_wands:
The wand reads a drawing like a sentence. There are seven element runes (Fire, Water, Wind, Earth, Light, Dark, Lightning) and six auxiliary signs: arrow, circle, triangle, spiral, square and the strike-through. Runes are not read turned: their orientation is part of the sign, and a Fire drawn askew easily becomes Light.

The first element rune is the core. Every further one amplifies it and also acts itself, at 40 % of its strength:
• the same rune again: power × 1.6
• Wind: reach × 1.5
• Earth: steadier, lasts 1.4 times as long
• Water: a larger area
• Fire: power × 1.3, but less steady
• Light: steadier
• Dark: lasts 1.5 times as long
• Lightning: power × 1.15, a slightly larger area
A line struck across a rune turns it around: Fire struck through cools and freezes, Wind struck through draws in instead of pushing away. Light and Dark cancel each other pair by pair, and Earth grounds Lightning the same way.

The auxiliary signs say where it acts. Without them the element pours from the hand up to 6 blocks ahead. An arrow places it at its tip, up to 24 blocks away; drawn upward means where I am looking. A rune running over the edge of a circle acts on myself. A triangle makes it burst all round, a spiral leaves it lying as a field that acts every second, a square lays it as a trap that waits up to two minutes for a step.

A circle with a rune wholly inside is a shield of that element, an empty circle a plain one. It absorbs 8 × power in harm and stands seven seconds (both longer with Earth or Dark). Projectiles stop at it, blows land on the shield, and whoever strikes an elemental shield feels its element at half strength. I cannot strike out of it. Add a spiral and it stays where it was raised: larger, three times as long, half again as strong, and players pass through.

Several circles, triangles or squares with runes in them are several spells at once. Below the parchment a line tells in advance what the drawing will do.

A spell does not simply work or fail; it is judged by three numbers shown after the cast.
• Accuracy: how close the strokes came to their runes. A careful hand reaches about 90 %, a hurried one about 70 %.
• Stability: accuracy plus the steadiness of the spell and the wand, less overload and hesitation (strokes over 2.5 seconds). Each unknown rune takes a fifth of it, each unreadable stroke two fifths.
• Power: 0.4 + 0.63 × accuracy; a fast, clean cast adds 3 %.

Stability decides the outcome: from 68 % it succeeds; from 50 % it comes out weakened (power × 0.6, distance × 0.7); from 32 % it fails by the worst-drawn rune: a poor core becomes the element it most resembled, a poor auxiliary sign sends it astray, a poor amplifier surges out of control. Below that it backfires and acts where I stand. None of this is chance: a failed Light heals, a strong Fire explodes, without breaking blocks.

A spell's tier is the number of its runes, auxiliary signs included. A wand carries a tier without harm:
• Wooden Wand: tier 2, steadiness +0, 64 durability
• Iron Wand: tier 4, steadiness +0.04, 250 durability
• Golden Wand: tier 5, steadiness +0.12, 120 durability
Every tier above that costs 0.15 stability. Each cast wears the wand by 1, plus 6 per tier of overload. Overloaded by four tiers, or worn out, it breaks and the spell loses its hold. Afterwards it rests briefly: 0.3 seconds plus 0.2 per rune.

Gear disturbs the hand too: each metal armour piece 0.02, the chestplate 0.04, a shield in the off hand 0.04, a two-handed weapon 0.03. Leather and cloth cost nothing. Rain weakens Fire and strengthens Water and Lightning; under open sky Light is stronger by day and Dark by night.

Runes are learned at the rune stones of old stone rings, about one in 48 chunks, or from a Rune Tome. An unknown rune still works, only less steadily; drawn at 60 % accuracy or better without fizzling, it is understood afterwards. Holding G draws without the parchment, in the middle of the view; a left click starts the next rune, letting go casts.

A sigil is a spell that stays lying on the ground and keeps working by itself. It is drawn like any spell, but its frame is two circles, one inside the other. Cast with a wand at solid ground within 6 blocks, it is inscribed there.

Structure:
• In the inner circle: the element, and around it a stabilising figure of 3 to 8 corners.
• In the ring between the circles: the instructions. Arrows give the direction, each short stroke +35 % strength, a small circle makes it act all round, a small triangle makes it burst, a small square makes it wait until someone comes within 2.5 blocks, a spiral makes it act twice as often.
• Wind in the ring lengthens its reach, Water widens its effect, Earth doubles its lifetime; Dark makes it act only on monsters, struck through only on my own side.

Capacity: every corner of the figure carries one instruction (Dark costs two). Each instruction beyond that costs 0.25 stability, each stroke that means nothing 0.08; without a figure a sigil holds only half as well. Its load on the wand is corners minus two: a triangle is light, an octagon tier 6. Overfull or without a figure and drawn poorly, it lies down and bursts 3 to 7 seconds later.

At work:
• If the arrows cancel out, the element hovers 1.3 blocks above it and acts every second on whatever comes into it.
• If they point somewhere, it shoots its element every 1.5 seconds, up to 16 blocks.
• A waiting sigil has 8 charges, two more per strength stroke.
• It lasts twenty minutes, a waiting one an hour, and keeps working after a restart.

Sneaking, use the wand on one sigil, then on a second within 24 blocks: now the first sets off the second, up to four links. A sigil is removed by hand at once, and is gone when its ground goes.

Nothing is left to chance at the enchanting table. With the piece in the main hand and Lapis Lazuli Powder in the pack, using the table opens a sitting: on the left the piece drawn large in its outline, on the right the runes lying ready. Every enchantment has its own rune, always the same.

Which runes lie ready is fixed, by bookshelves and by the levels held on sitting down:
• common (Protection, Sharpness, Efficiency, Power): 0 shelves, level 1, costs 1 level
• uncommon (Unbreaking and others): 4 shelves, level 8, costs 2
• rare (Fortune, Looting, Fire Aspect and others): 9 shelves, level 16, costs 3
• very rare and treasures (Silk Touch, Mending and others): 15 shelves, level 25, costs 4
What lay ready on sitting down stays ready until the sitting ends.

A rune is picked up, turned with a right click, the mouse wheel or R, and laid on the piece. With 90 % of it on the piece it gives the highest level, less in proportion; if that is not enough for one level it does nothing. Runes may touch, may not overlap, and may hang over the edge. On iron, bronze, steel and every part a common rune is 9 × 9 squares, a rare one 11 × 11; on a small piece, which rune gets the room is my choice. The old exclusions do not hold: Protection lies beside Fire Protection, Fortune beside Silk Touch. Only the same rune twice is refused.

• Parts first: on a blade, a pickaxe head or a piece of armour plate a rune works in fully and goes on into the finished piece. On a finished tool it reaches one level below the highest.
• How many runes a piece holds depends on its metal: gold 6, copper 5, iron, bronze and steel 4. Good smithing adds more: one from 75 % craftsmanship, two from 100 %, three from 125 %.
• Cost: one measure of powder per six squares written, plus 1 to 4 levels per rune.

A piece can return to the table again and again. Old runes stay where they lie; a right click marks one to be wiped, which costs nothing but gives nothing back. Librarians no longer sell enchanted books, and three in four books from chests are gone.
journal.hardwrought.lore.oil_and_current:
Current runs out along the wire and back through the earth; a single wire is already a circuit. Voltages and currents are worked out exactly twice a second. The Voltmeter, held to any point, shows voltage, current and how hard the wires are working.

The Dynamo gives 2 volts for every turn per minute: a Hand Crank at 16 RPM gives 32 V, 32 RPM give 64 V. Voltage is bought with gearing, current with strength, for every ampere makes it 6 stress units per RPM heavier to turn. A Water Wheel in a good river runs about four lamps, a hand on a crank one, and dimly. If the driveline cannot hold the current, the dynamo lets go for five seconds and then tries again: lamps that flash every few seconds hang on an overloaded dynamo.

Dynamos, batteries and machines take no wire themselves; a Copper Coil set against any face is their connection. Lamps, insulators and line masts take wire directly. Every point holds four wires, one coil strings 8 blocks, and nothing may stand in the way. Shears take wires off.
• Copper Wire: 0.04 Ω per block, 4 A, spans 16
• Copper Cable: 0.01 Ω per block, 16 A, spans 24
• Insulated Wire: like copper wire, but it does not bite and goes through walls; spans 12

The Electric Lamp has 120 Ω and is made for 60 V: there it draws half an ampere and gives full light. Below that it dims, and under 12 V it stays dark. Above 75 V its filament strains, and at 110 V it goes at once; copper wire used on a dead lamp winds it a new one.

The Battery is a source of its own: 54 V empty to 62 V full, behind 2 Ω. It charges only from a line above its own voltage, so never from a hand crank, but from 64 V it does, and it feeds the line once it falls below. It holds 72,000 watt-seconds, two lamps for twenty minutes, and gives back four fifths. More than 8 A in or out boils the acid, and kept up, the case bursts.

Every machine on current is made for 60 V and takes current only while something lies in it and there is room for what it makes; standing idle it takes nothing.
• Basic Crusher: 1.5 A, 2 seconds a piece
• Electric Furnace: 2 A, 5 seconds
• Sawmill: 1.5 A, 3 seconds, half as many boards again
• Plate Press: 2 A, 4 seconds
On less voltage it works by the square: half the voltage, a quarter of the work. Under 30 V it only hums. Above 75 V it runs faster but its windings cook; at 110 V they burn out at once, and copper wire rewinds them. Hoppers feed it from the top and sides and draw from the bottom.

Bearings and gaskets wear: oiled, through in ten hours of work, dry six times as fast. Oil lasts two hours of work, and a bottle of Machine Oil (made from heavy oil) fills it again. Worn, it works slower, down to half, and smokes; worn through, it seizes until a Service Kit puts new bearings and gaskets in.

Bare wire from 30 V bites whatever touches it: a twentieth of the voltage in half hearts, twice a second, and armour is no help. Water at a point leaks current through 20 Ω, and everything standing in water within four blocks is shocked; rain does the same more gently to a dynamo or lamp under open sky, and one block above is roof enough. An overloaded wire glows and parts, a quarter over its rating after about a quarter of a minute, at twice its rating after three seconds, and what drips from it sets fire to what lies below.

Protection:
• Fuse Box: opens after half a second at half again its 4 A, sooner than the wire behind it burns; a new Fuse Cartridge mends it.
• Breaker: trips at 16 A and is closed again by hand.
• Knife Switch: thrown by hand or following a redstone signal; it is set down open.
A Transformer (1:4) lifts 60 V to 240 V: the same power on a quarter of the current, with a sixteenth of the loss.

Item pipes, eight from three metal plates, carry items. Each pipe holds one batch and hands it on after a set time:
• Item Pipe (Bronze): one item a second
• Item Pipe (Iron): four every half second, eight times as much
A run is as fast as its slowest pipe. A batch goes to the nearest block that takes it, chest, furnace or machine, but never back into the one it came from. If nothing takes it, it waits in the pipe. Hoppers and other blocks that push items may fill in on any side.

The Pipe Wrench sets each side of a pipe on its own, used on the arm or that face of the core:
• towards a block: filling (default), drawing (orange ring), cut off, filling again
• towards another pipe: joined or cut off
A drawing side takes a batch out of its block whenever the pipe is empty, at its metal's pace, and never fills that block. So a pipe under a machine empties its output by itself and carries the crusher's powder on to the electric furnace.

Fluid pipes, eight from plate, glass pane and plate, carry oil and all that comes of it: bronze 100 mB a second, iron 250. A pipe holds nothing itself; what is drawn goes at once to the nearest taker.
• Downhill it runs by itself: out of a tank, 100 mB a second for every block of drop. Two tanks on one level even out.
• Uphill needs a pump. The Mechanical Pump on a shaft, gear or crank pushes 250 mB a second at 16 RPM, in proportion to speed; without a running pump an uphill run stands still.
• A Tank holds 16 buckets of one liquid; buckets fill and empty it, an empty hand reads it, and so does a comparator.
A drawing side takes from a tank, from the drilling rig, or from an oil lake beside it, there a bucket at a time.

Oil and gas lie only under sedimentary rock, in reservoirs between Y -48 and Y 16, flat and 40 to 96 blocks across; not every region has one, and some hold natural gas alone. Struck against natural rock while sneaking, a pickaxe names the rock. Standing over a reservoir, it tells what lies below and where its top is; nearby, even a plain pickaxe smells traces, while an iron or diamond pickaxe gives bearing and distance up to 160 blocks. The top is domed, so the way down is shortest over the middle.

The Drilling Rig takes 12 stress units per RPM, 192 at 16 RPM, more than a hand crank gives. It then bores half a block a second; over empty ground it bores to the bottom of the world and comes up dry. When it strikes, a rush of gas comes first. A fresh well gives up to 50 mB of oil a second at 16 RPM, times its pressure; every reservoir is finite, and as it empties the pressure falls to a twentieth. Its tank holds 16 buckets; an empty bucket draws from it, a Gas Canister takes 16 units. Gas beyond 64 units goes up a Gas Pipe set on top of the rig and out, or without a pipe as methane around the rig. At 128 it backs up and the well stops.

The Refinery Base stands over fire, lava, magma, a lit furnace, campfire, forge or a gas burner, holds 8 buckets of crude oil and boils 100 mB every second:
• base: 15 mB bitumen
• tray 1: 25 heavy oil
• tray 2: 25 diesel
• tray 3: 10 kerosene
• tray 4: 20 naphtha
• tray 5: 2 units of LPG
What would condense above the topmost tray is flared off. Each tray holds 4 buckets; when one is full, the whole column waits. So a bucket of diesel costs 4 buckets of crude oil and 40 seconds.

The Diesel Generator gives 64 V through a copper coil. It burns 0.25 mB a second idling and 1 mB per kilojoule given; at 500 W a bucket lasts a good twenty minutes. Kerosene goes 90 % as far, the still's fuel 75 %. Redstone stops it, and its exhaust belongs out through a gas pipe.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_nether_cros:
A frame of real obsidian opens only an unstable portal. It takes the traveller through, and nothing else:

• Everything in the inventory, armour included, stays behind on the side being left. It is not lost: come back to that side and every piece lies in its old slot again, the armour back on. Where a slot is taken, it goes elsewhere or drops at the feet.
• Only packs, with what is in them, and the smithing gloves come along.
• No portal forms on the other side. The traveller is set down on safe ground near where it would have formed; going into the Nether, in the nearest Ash Grove if one lies within 640 blocks. Where there is no footing at all, a small floor of netherrack is made.
• Anything that is not a player does not go through at all, not even a thrown item.

An unstable portal crackles with sparks and smoke; a stable one is quiet.

Whoever enters the Nether respawns there from then on. Dying does not take them home to their bed and chests. The old spawn point is kept and applies again as soon as they come home through a portal.

On arrival, and after every respawn in the Nether, Heat Resistance lasts fifteen minutes.

About the frame: water on lava gives only cast obsidian. Like obsidian it wants a steel pickaxe, and a frame of it will not light. It becomes real in the smeltery, a minute per block at 1600 degrees: coal with bellows (up to 1650 degrees) or lava will do.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_nether_heat:
The Nether's air stands at a good 35 degrees, and it is hotter near lava, fire, blazes and magma cubes. The body takes 20 degrees as comfortable; anything above drives its warmth up, and above 28 degrees it also costs water.

While Heat Resistance lasts, the hot side of the air does not reach the body at all. After that, armour has to carry it.

The Ash Grove is the exception: about 19 degrees, grey Nether grass, drifting ash, no lava. Where the lava sea lies elsewhere, here lies a lake of boiled water, edged with cast obsidian towards the lava. It is as common as any other Nether biome.

• Water: only in the Ash Grove does poured water stay, and it is always purified, standing or flowing. Everywhere else a bucket hisses empty.
• Ashcork: grows on netherrack and soul soil, in the dark, and does not burn. An axe strips two ashcork bark from every log.
• Bark armour: it pulls hot air towards comfort and leaves cold alone. A full set takes three quarters of the excess, so 36 degrees feel like 24. Single pieces count by area: cap 15, tunic 40, leggings 30, boots 15 in a hundred. Against blows, bark does little.

The drying rack works in the Nether without sky, by day and night, and six times as fast.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_nether_fres:
The Nether lacks the Overworld's stone and clay, but everything a fresh start needs lies close:

• Netherrack, Nether grass, nylium and soul soil can be dug by hand, slowly.
• Gravel gives flint. Blackstone breaks into blackstone pieces under a pickaxe; a stone pickaxe, stone hatchet and hammer are made of them as of cobblestone pieces.
• Nether coal, copper, tin and iron ore sit all through the netherrack. They give what their kin above give; coal wants a flint pickaxe, the rest a stone one.
• Ashcork leaves give fibre and sticks. The first workbench is hewn from an ashcork log with an iron axe.
• Chests in fortresses, bastions and ruined portals often hold a start: flint shards, leaf cord, sticks, coal, raw copper, raw iron, blackstone pieces and ashcork saplings.

There is no clay for a brick furnace. Instead a magma block heats metal thrown onto it, in the Nether only. Every half second the piece closes twelve hundredths of the gap to its goal, but at least 15 degrees. The goal is the top of its working heat, at most 1300 degrees: iron gets just that far, copper, bronze and gold to the top of their range. Nothing is spoiled. What wants forging hotter is still the forge's work.

Magic feels the place too: water spells work at half strength here, fire spells a fifth stronger.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_nether_stab:
A portal is stable when at least two running stabilisers sit against its frame: in the frame's plane up to one block beyond it, or right in front of or behind it. Then it takes everything its traveller carries, and a portal forms on the other side.

What counts is always the portal one leaves through. The new portal on the other side starts out unstable itself; going back with gear needs stabilisers of its own there.

Provisional portal stabiliser: four blackstone pieces, two Nether quartz and two gold nuggets around a magma block. It runs on the heat around it: always in the Nether, elsewhere only where lava or a magma block touches it directly. It checks every two seconds and whenever something beside it changes. So a magma block beside it keeps it running in the Overworld too.

Portal stabiliser: the provisional one, surrounded by four Nether quartz, two gold ingots and two blaze rods. It runs anywhere, on current from 48 volts, fed like a machine through a copper coil set against it; no wire goes to it directly. At 96 ohms it draws half an ampere at 48 volts, as much as a lamp. If the voltage drops below 48 volts it stops, and the portal turns unstable.

How to tell:
• A running provisional one glows and throws embers; a running electric one glows, sparks and hums.
• A wisp is drawn from each running one into the portal.
• A stable portal does not crackle; crossing it says "Stable Portal – Everything came through".
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_wither_skul:
Wither skeletons guard the Nether fortresses. One in five carries a bow and fights as an archer, and its arrows burn; the rest come with the blade.

A wither skeleton skull is empty when it drops. It is charged like this:
• Light soul fire, that is, fire on soul sand or soul soil.
• Throw the skull in. It does not burn there.
• Leave it for half a minute. Souls are seen going into it, more the fuller it gets. Done, it shimmers as if enchanted.

Good to know:
• A whole stack charges at once. Throwing all three skulls in together saves time.
• A skull taken out too early keeps what it has already drunk and goes on charging next time.
• The charge stays when the skull is placed, broken and picked up again.

On the T of four soul sand or soul soil blocks, the Wither rises only if all three skulls are charged. Otherwise the empty ones smoke, and there is a hiss.

The Wither essence it leaves on dying is an ink of its own at the enchanting table: it writes only the Soulbound rune, two measures per rune, and that rune can be written in nothing else. A piece bound so stays in its slot through a death and is there again on waking; the rune is spent then, the others stay.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_wither_figh:
The Wither can do all it always could, and more:

• It breaks load-bearing blocks, and what stood on them comes down by the rules of the statics. So fight it far from anything worth keeping.
• At half its health it calls three wither skeletons, at a quarter three more.
• It jumps: on average every ten to twenty seconds it vanishes in souls and smoke and appears six to fourteen blocks beside its target, three to eight blocks above. Walled in by what it cannot break, say bedrock over its head and on three sides, it jumps at once. It cannot be trapped.
• Soul storm: below a quarter of its health it drains every player within 16 blocks. Each second there adds three seconds of Drain.

Drain: breath comes back slower and hunger comes faster, at level I by a fifth and a quarter, at level II twice, at level III three times as much. Level II holds from 45 seconds left, III from 100; no more than 180 seconds build up. Every point of damage from the Wither and its skulls adds ten seconds as well. So do not linger in the storm: in, strike, out.

Its death: a last great blast, stronger than TNT. Keep away. Then its souls gather from all around for four seconds, and the nether star hangs floating where it died. It does not fall and does not vanish. Below it lie three to five Wither essence.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_underworld_:
The seal:
• The seal stone must stand in the Overworld below y -180.
• Two blocks out diagonally, at all four corners and level with it, stands a pillar of worked deepslate (chiseled, polished, bricks or tiles, cracked ones too), each with a soul lantern on it.
• If anything is missing, the stone says so when the nether star is offered.

The star burns out, and over five seconds the ground cracks ring by ring up to four blocks out. A pit three blocks deep remains with the shaft at its bottom, open for good and for everyone. Water running into it is swallowed by the shaft. Whoever steps in falls into the Underworld.

The way back: ruins in every Underworld biome hold dim ascent shafts in rings of deepslate bricks. A pale shard rekindles one for good and is used up. Standing two seconds in its light carries one up, to beside the shaft one came down through; stepping out starts the count over. Only the first descent ends under the seal; every later one ends beside the ascent shaft one last went up from.

Pale shards grow as faintly glowing clusters (light 6) on the rock walls of the Echo Chasm, one or two per chunk, in the Stone Wastes only in one chunk in eight. A cluster gives one to three shards, or itself with Silk Touch.

Once the Witch King is beaten, his throne is a third way: sit on it (two seconds, sneaking cancels) and one stands by its seat in the Overworld. The first time, the seat is set down beside one's bed, or at world spawn without one. Sitting on the seat leads down to the foot of the throne. The seat cannot be broken; sneaking with an empty hand picks it up to set it down elsewhere.

The Underworld is a cave world between bedrock floor and roof, with no sky, day or weather. The air stands around 6 degrees and grows warmer further down. There is no light of its own and no getting used to the dark: without a lamp it stays black, and only what glows can be seen.

• Stone Wastes: bare banded rock, very rich in ore, which lies open on the walls. Hardly any light, no glow lichen.
• Overgrown Halls: wild cave growth, the only food down here.
• Dripstone Depths: stalactites break loose by themselves, a crack, trickling dust, then the fall. On average one nearby every fifteen seconds.
• Mossy Grove: glow berries and quiet, the safest place.
• Graveyard and Ossuary: the only places anything spawns. Grave walkers (28 health, armoured, slow; their bite opens wounds and one time in three carries grave dirt in) and grave skeletons (an old bow, or two times in five a worn iron sword) rise out of the ground: for a second the soil stirs, then they dig their way out for two seconds and do nothing else. Time to strike.
• Flooded Halls: black lakes up to y 8, their water swamp water.
• Echo Chasm: deep chasms with ledges, every sound coming back twice.
• Deep Dark: as above, with ancient cities and the Warden.

The ruins hold little, and that worn: stale bread, bad water, worn tools, candles, torches, bandages, and now and then one of eight journals of those who came before.

Eyes in the dark, footsteps not one's own, breathing, a light going out behind, the spinning compass: none of it does harm. Magic, though, feels the place: light spells work at only seven tenths, dark spells three tenths stronger.

Adamantium lies only in the Underworld's Stone Wastes: three small veins per chunk of at most four blocks, between y -56 and 64, often open on the cave walls. A steel pickaxe or better breaks it. Mithril, by contrast, lies in the Overworld, deep down between y -180 and -64.

Melting:
• Mithril melts at 1900 degrees; coke alone (up to 2000 degrees) is enough.
• Adamantium melts only at 2600 degrees. For that the smeltery needs coke and bellows, together up to 4200 degrees; coal reaches only 1650 even with bellows.
• A whole ore block is worth two ingots in the smeltery.

Above netherite nothing is forged any more, only upgraded. A mithril or adamant upgrade template is made of four ingots of the metal around a cast blank. At the smithing table: the piece in the main hand, template and ingot in the inventory, use the table. Netherite becomes mithril, mithril becomes adamant; template and ingot are used up.

Then the pattern is traced, for mithril a figure of eight in 15 seconds, for adamant a spiral in 18. Take hold of the glowing point and follow the line with the button held. Within 2.5 pixels the trace counts as true, from 7.5 (mithril) or 6 (adamant) as missed; straying more than 14 loses the line, to be taken up again. The upgrade always succeeds, and runes, hardening and polish stay. The accuracy decides the craftsmanship: 75 percent changes nothing, every point above adds 0.6 points (at most +15), every point below takes 0.6 (at most -30).

• Mithril: 3400 durability, armour 4/7/9/4, toughness 4; takes runes more readily than adamant.
• Adamant: 4800 durability, armour 4/8/10/4, toughness 5; the fastest tool, the heaviest blow.
Neither burns.

His citadel is a round hall at the bottom of the Ossuary, at most one per 256 by 256 blocks. Entering the hall wakes him: souls gather for five seconds, then he steps out of a rift, untouchable for three seconds. He has 500 health. His harm is hex: armour holds none of it, only half against his blows; protective runes count half, at most 40 instead of 80 percent. A shield drawn with the wand stops everything while its strength lasts, but one's own arrows too.

• Down to two thirds: he hovers, keeps his distance and slips away through rifts when one comes within seven blocks. Melee does only a quarter, bow and spells hit in full. Spectral swords (8 damage) fly one by one, in a fan (dodge sideways) or from a ring closing in (get out).
• Then he hangs behind a ward over the middle, invulnerable; damage beyond the threshold is lost. Four soul crystals stand at the corners, an arrow or a few blows break each. He rains swords from sigils, sends hunting souls, calls up his dead, draws a line of light and drives his lance along it a second and a half later (14), and breaks the floor open in spokes: stand between them. Each violet mark erupts just over a second later (9, throws up). Each crystal makes him quicker and tears the floor open round whoever broke it; the fourth breaks the ward.
• The curse: from then on every 21 seconds (26 later, seven less in his rage) he gathers it for four seconds and strikes everyone within 40 blocks for 18. Raise the shield then.
• At last he grows to a giant and can be struck. Red marks show blows (18, up to three in a row) and leaps (12 within 7); besides, shockwaves, lines of eruptions and rifts at one's back. Below 30 percent he rages.

Going more than 48 blocks away lets him heal; after 30 seconds alone he returns whole to his throne.

He leaves his mantle and four to eight pale shards. The mantle glides like elytra; holding jump drives it on and wears it, pale shards mend it. Jumping twice in the air (or X) lets one fly as in creative mode, jump to rise and sneak to sink, for 20 seconds on a full charge (sinking costs a fifth), eight seconds of gliding or standing refill it. More than 64 blocks above the ground, it gives out for five seconds.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_end_arrival:
Whoever steps through the End portal does not land on an island. Every traveller is set down at X 150, Y 90, Z 0, far out in the void, facing west towards the broken island. Beneath them lies a Light over the Void, a floor five blocks by five. It holds like stone, but only for thirty seconds. In its last ten seconds it flickers violet and counts each second down. Then it is gone. Every new passage through the portal lights it afresh.

While the dragon lives, a hard law holds in the End: no block can be placed and no bucket emptied. This holds from the first visit until the first dragon falls, and again whenever one has been raised. Pillaring, bridging, catching a fall with a block: none of it works. Only the Mantle of the Witch King keeps you up.

For the mantle in the End:
• A full soul charge gives twenty seconds of hovering. Gliding or standing fills it again in eight seconds. Sinking costs only a fifth as much.
• The ceiling is fixed at Y 160. Eight blocks below it you can feel the air thinning. Fly above it and the mantle fails for five seconds, and you fall.

Only fragments are left of the old main island. The middle one carries the exit portal. It is flat on top, with its top at Y 62, and reaches about 18 blocks out. Around it hang eighteen smaller fragments between Y 44 and Y 96, up to 112 blocks from the middle, and further out some forty loose stones. The obsidian pillars stand alone in the void and end 34 blocks below their tops in a jagged point. You can land on the fragments, refill your charge and fight on foot. Not all of them last the whole fight.

Whoever dies in the End wakes in the Overworld as usual, and has to fly in again through portal and void.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_end_crystal:
While even one End Crystal stands on a pillar, the dragon is shielded. Only a fifth of each blow reaches it. On top of that, the crystals heal it as they always have. So the crystals must fall first.

Each crystal carries its own ward. The ward holds 40 damage, or 60 around a raised dragon. Every hit from blade, arrow or spell takes its damage off the ward, and the crystal itself is unharmed. Fire does not touch the ward. When the ward reaches zero it shatters with a sound like breaking glass. Only the next hit breaks the crystal. It bursts and throws every player within about ten blocks away, so do not hover too close to it. While the dragon is less than 48 blocks from the crystal, the ward mends by one and a half points a second, even if it was already broken. So it pays to go for a crystal when the dragon is circling at the far side, and to break it in one go.

The fight has four stages:
• The crystals: while one stands. The dragon attacks with bolts, gusts and the occasional dive.
• The hunt: all crystals are gone. Now clouds and summonings join in, and it dives more often.
• The landing: below 55 % health it lands now and then on the middle fragment. Then you can face it on foot.
• The breaking: below 25 % it rages. It hits 15 % harder, rests for less time, marks its dives more briefly and often climbs straight into a second one. About every eleven and a half seconds a fragment, usually one near its prey, crumbles and falls into the void, and the middle one loses stones from its edge. Every three and a half seconds the void drags anyone not standing on solid ground downwards.

Between attacks it circles wide around the middle, about 58 blocks out. These rests get shorter with each stage. It hunts anyone closer than 170 blocks to the middle. Usually it picks the nearest and stays on them for a while.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_end_dragon_:
After every rest the dragon picks an attack, never the same one twice in a row. Every attack is announced before it lands.

• Bolts: it passes its prey to the side and fires four void bolts, six when raging. They aim where you are about to be and steer after you for a moment. Where they burst, a void cloud hangs for seven seconds. A hit costs 12. A bolt can be shot down, and then it bursts where it is.
• Gust: it comes close, holds still and draws breath under its wings. Then it beats them: a cone of wind 28 blocks long throws everyone in it far away and down. Damage 7.
• Dive: it climbs high above its prey. A sigil and a pillar of light mark the target about a second ahead. Then it falls. Its head strikes for 22, and anyone within six blocks of the mark is torn away. So move away from the mark, don't just dodge the head.
• Clouds: from the hunt on, it flies past its prey and breathes five clouds into the air. Each lasts eight seconds and blocks the way.
• Summon: from the hunt on, at most every 30 seconds. It roars, and up to three endermen appear on fragments near its prey. Never more than six at once.
• Landing: see the stages.

A bite costs 16. Brushing against its wings or body costs 6 and throws you aside.

On harm: bite, dive, brushing and stamping are blows, and armour holds only half against them. Bolts, gust and clouds are void, and armour does not hold against them at all. Protective runes hold half against either. A cloud bites for 4 every half second. Every hit throws its victim away and knocks them out of the hover. You have to catch the fall yourself. So never fight right over the abyss if you can help it.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_end_landing:
The landing: below 55 % health the dragon comes down on the exit portal in the middle. The landing alone shakes the ground. While down, it keeps its head turned towards its prey.
• Stamp: first a magenta mark appears around it, about eleven blocks wide. Shortly after, the ground quakes. Whoever stands in the mark takes 15 and is thrown upwards. At the same time stones break off the fragment's edge.
• Breath: seven violet marks form an arc in front of it, towards its prey. Shortly after, void clouds lie there.
It rises again once it has lost 15 % of its full health, or after 13 seconds at the latest, 10 when raging. After that it lands again no sooner than 26 seconds later, 18 when raging. Be ready and hit hard, and the landing ends quickly.

When the first dragon dies, it leaves the Dragon Egg. The building ban is lifted, and the End lies open.

The return: four End Crystals on the edges of the exit portal call the dragon back. The spectacle takes a while. First the void stirs above the portal for about five seconds. Then the pillars are raised again, one after another, two seconds each. Then comes the summoning, again about five seconds, and finally the dragon breaks free. As soon as it lives, the building ban holds again.

The raised dragon:
• has 900 health instead of 600,
• hits 30 % harder, and another 15 % when raging,
• rests less and fires faster bolts, two more per volley,
• marks its dive more briefly from the start and often dives a second time straight away,
• when raging, crumbles a fragment every nine seconds,
• from the hunt on, has a new attack, skyfall: six marks light up around each of up to three foes. Right after, a void bolt falls on each mark from the sky.

Its crystal wards hold 60. When it dies, about ten seconds later its Dragon Heart appears above the portal. It glows, cannot be destroyed and never despawns. Only a raised dragon leaves one.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_ritual_void:
Void crystal grows like amethyst, but only deep down. Its geodes lie only in the Overworld, between the bottom of the world and about Y −80. They are rare, roughly one in 64 chunks. Outside they have a shell of smooth basalt, with calcite beneath. Inside they are lined with Blocks of Void Crystal. Here and there among them sits a Budding Void Crystal, humming darkly.

Growth:
• Only Budding Void Crystal sprouts anything. On random ticks it puts out a small bud on one of its faces, which grows into a medium and a large bud and finally into a Void Crystal Cluster.
• Budding Void Crystal cannot be taken away. Mined, it is gone, even with Silk Touch. So the geode is a plantation where it lies. Leave it standing.
• Buds that are not yet clusters give nothing without Silk Touch. With Silk Touch you get the bud itself.
• A full cluster gives four Void Crystal Shards to a pickaxe, and Fortune raises that. Without the right tool, or when it breaks by itself, it gives two.

What to make of it:
• Four shards in a square make a Block of Void Crystal, one of the eight offerings.
• One shard goes into the Ritual Altar.
• A shard and an Ink Sac make two Void Ink. A rune written in Void Ink stands one level above its enchantment's highest, and the piece holds two more runes.
• A Mithril Wand, two shards and an Echo Shard make the Void Crystal Wand. It carries spells up to tier 8, and overload costs it only half as much stability.

A Block of Void Crystal drops itself when mined. So if you placed it too soon, you lose nothing. It pays to let a geode grow for a while and harvest it several times, rather than knocking everything off on the first visit.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_ritual_temp:
The ritual needs a temple. It is built block by block from one of the three projections in the book, anywhere you like:
• Temple of the Plains: white quartz and stone under a green copper dome.
• Temple of the Desert: sandstone, lapis and gold under a stepped pyramid.
• Temple of the Rock: deepslate, tuff and amethyst under a tall pointed spire.
Each is 59 blocks across and up to 40 high. It has a terrace with stairs on all four sides, a colonnade with gates, four corner towers, and in the middle the round ritual hall with eight pillars. Its roof is open to the sky at the top. Which of the three it is, the building itself decides. The altar recognises whichever is furthest along.

The Ritual Altar comes first, in the exact middle of the hall to be. It is made from two Blocks of Gold, an Eye of Ender, two Crying Obsidian, a Void Crystal Shard and three Polished Blackstone Bricks. It holds the temple up: under the building rules stone reaches out only two blocks, copper five. No dome over the hall could stand that way. But every block lying exactly where the plan wants it counts to the physics as anchored, like natural ground. This holds up to 29 blocks sideways from the altar, 8 below and 40 above. Without the altar, or for anything not in the plan, the ordinary physics apply. If the altar is broken, the temple loses that hold.

The courtyard between colonnade and hall, and the foundation under the terrace, are left free. The plan shows a garden there, but does not ask for one. On the paths, the plan's two path stones can stand in for each other.

The temple stands once 98 % of the required blocks are right. So a stray block will not bring it down. Right-click the altar to see how far the building has come: the share in percent, the number of wrong blocks and where the nearest one is. At the same time every block still wrong is marked red in the world, with the wanted block drawn over it, up to 4096 at once, nearest first. Each mark vanishes as soon as its block is right.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_ritual_offe:
Eight Offering Pedestals stand in a ring around the altar, one level lower than it, about six and a half blocks from its middle. They stand between the hall's eight pillars. Each is made from a Gold Ingot, a Chiseled Polished Blackstone and three Polished Blackstone Bricks. A pedestal binds to an altar only when it stands on one of the plan's eight places. Placed anywhere else, it wants nothing.

Each place wants its own offering. Seen from the altar, the ring starts just south of east and runs clockwise:
• Nether Star, for the Wither
• Dragon Egg, from the first dragon
• Pale Shard, from the Underworld
• Block of Void Crystal
• Adamantium Ingot, from the forge
• Electric Motor, from the electric line
• Bucket of Diesel, from the refinery
• Golden Wand, from magic
You do not need to remember the order. Above each empty pedestal floats a pale image of what it wants. Right-click it with an empty hand to have it named in words too.

Rules for offering:
• Any of the eight offerings held to a pedestal is only laid down or refused, never used. No diesel is poured out, no wand is cast. Hold the wrong one, and the pedestal says what it wants.
• Each pedestal holds exactly one item, which then floats above it, slowly turning.
• Until the ritual begins, right-clicking with an empty hand takes the offering back. If a pedestal is broken, its offering drops.
• If the altar disappears, the pedestal forgets what it wanted until one stands again.

The altar keeps count: once the temple stands, a right-click tells you how many offerings are still missing and which comes next. When all are laid, it says: "All offerings are in place." The Dragon Egg comes only from the first dragon. Throw it away and there is no second one, so guard it well.
journal.hardwrought.lore.the_ritual_last:
The Dragon Heart, laid on the altar, begins the ritual. For that the temple must stand and every offering must be in place. If anything is missing, the altar names it and does not take the heart.

The ritual lasts a little over a minute:
• At once night draws in: under a sky with days, time races towards midnight.
• After one second the pedestals kindle one after another, a little over a second apart, and each sends a beam to the altar.
• After 12 seconds the heart rises above the altar. Rings of light rise around it.
• From 15 seconds, lightning strikes all round the temple, 18 to 34 blocks out. It is only for show and harms nothing and no one.
• After 24 seconds a pillar of light rises through the open roof into the sky.
• After 45 seconds the eight offerings burn away into light. Then a heart beats, faster and faster.
• After 55 seconds everything comes at once: a wave of light over the land, fireworks, and morning. The clock jumps to the next day.

The chamber binds: anyone within twelve and a half blocks of the altar is bound to the ritual. This includes anyone who comes in while it runs. Whoever tries to pass through the wall, or rise more than ten blocks above the altar, bounces off a ward and is set back inside. So if you want to take part, be inside the hall already. Whoever stays outside watches.

At the end, everyone bound rises through the open roof into the sky. Meanwhile they cannot be hurt and do not fall. A golden outline kindles around them, and at the height of it light breaks out of them. From then on they are in creative mode, and flying. The game says thank you.

If the world is left in the middle of the ritual, it stops. The heart stays on the altar. A right-click on the altar then begins it again from the start. If the altar is broken before the end, the heart drops. Once the ritual is complete, the heart floats above the altar for good. The altar cannot be lit a second time.
journal.hardwrought.first_edge.title: Something with an edge
journal.hardwrought.first_edge.text: My hands do nothing against rock or standing timber. Leaves pulled apart by hand give sticks and now and then a green fibre. Gravel dug by hand gives flint shards. A shard, a stick and the fibre, put together in my own hands, make a hatchet: no bench needed. With it I can cut logs. If I am thirsty, I crouch at a river and drink from my empty hand.
journal.hardwrought.something_to_carry.t: My hands and my belt hold nine things and not one more. The green fibre has to dry in the sun on a rack of sticks before it twists into cord. A stick rubbed long enough on stone comes to a point, a needle. With cord and a needle, cloth can be woven, and cloth sewn into a pack.
journal.hardwrought.fire_by_friction.tex: Sticks and split logs, put together in my hands, make a fire pit. It is set down cold. Two crossed sticks, also made in my hands, are spun against it until it catches. A burning fire cooks meat, fires clay and keeps the night back.
journal.hardwrought.fibre_and_cord.title: Cord from leaves
journal.hardwrought.fibre_and_cord.text: Green fibre binds a tool as it is, but it will not twist. Sticks and fibre in my hands make a drying rack. Set out under open sky, it dries the fibre into cord in half a day of sun; rain and night stop it. I will need cord for a mallet, for bandages and much more.
journal.hardwrought.light_against_the_da: The flint pick is poor, but it breaks stone and coal. Coal on a stick, made in my hands, is a torch, though it gives no light until I hold it to a burning fire. Lit, it burns for about a day, in my hand or on the wall, and then it is ash. I should always carry a spare.
journal.hardwrought.firmer_than_flint.te: Flint blunts after a few blows, and it will not break iron ore. Cobblestone from the flint pick breaks apart in my hands into pieces of rock. Pieces, a stick and fibre make a stone pick and a stone hatchet, still in my own hands. The stone pick is what iron ore asks for.
